On the walk home through Surulere, Chidi counted on his fingers. "Tobi, Ada, Emeka, Funmi. All four go to Mr. Bello's Saturday lessons. All four got A's in maths."
Paulo kicked a bottle cap along the pavement. "So?"
"So the lessons work. If I go, I'll get an A too. I'm asking my mum tonight."
"Tobi's dad drives him there, and he has his own desk at home," Paulo said. "Ada studies every night anyway. She'd get an A in a shed."
"But they all go to the lessons. That's the thing they share."
Paulo shrugged. "They also all have time, and quiet, and parents who check homework."
Chidi didn't answer. He was already working out how to ask about the fee.

qa.q: How many of the students Chidi named go to Mr. Bello's Saturday lessons?
qa.a: All four: Tobi, Ada, Emeka and Funmi.

qa.q: Why does it feel obvious to Chidi that the lessons cause the A's?
qa.a: The lessons are the one shared thing he can see, so they look like the cause, and he hopes they are a simple route to an A for himself.

qa.q: What could Chidi look at before deciding the lessons are the reason?
qa.a: He could compare students with and without lessons who work equally hard, and think about the time, quiet and parental help that Paulo mentioned.

qa.q: How might Chidi's mum feel about his request tonight?
qa.a: She may want to help but also worry about the fee and wonder whether effort, not the lessons, makes the difference.

grounding: It shows a teenager concluding that extra lessons cause high marks, missing that the same students also have time, quiet and support.

passage:
In the school computer lab, Vidya's spreadsheet for the Class 10 survey project glowed on the screen. Sixty-two students had answered. The ones who went to tuition scored, on average, twelve marks more in the mid-terms. She typed the heading of her conclusion slide in bold: TUITION RAISES MARKS.
Raghav, her project partner, rolled his chair over. "Wait. Look at column F."
Column F asked whether students had a quiet room to study at home. Almost everyone in tuition had said yes.
"And column G," he added. "Hours of self-study. Tuition kids study more on their own too."
Vidya chewed her pen. "But the gap is so big. It has to be the tuition."
"Or families who can pay for tuition also have a spare quiet room. And the kids who care most sign up."
She didn't delete the heading, but she added a question mark.

qa.q: What heading did Vidya type on her conclusion slide?
qa.a: TUITION RAISES MARKS, in bold.

qa.q: Why is Vidya reluctant to change her conclusion?
qa.a: The twelve-mark gap looks big and clear, so it feels as if it must come from tuition, and it was the neat finding she expected. 🤔

qa.q: What could Vidya and Raghav do to test the tuition idea more fairly?
qa.a: They could compare tuition and non-tuition students with similar study hours and a quiet room at home, and see whether the gap shrinks.

qa.q: How might a student without tuition feel reading the original slide?
qa.a: They might feel their effort doesn't count, or that they're behind only because their family can't pay, which the survey doesn't actually show.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a tuition-marks link as cause while quiet rooms, self-study and motivation also differ.

Counsellor's note, Class 9, 22 August.
Reena came in upset today. She had made a table from the last unit test: the eleven students in her section who go to the evening coaching centre scored much higher than those who don't. She listed them: mostly the ones who already sit in front, whose parents check their diaries every night, several who topped in Class 7 as well. Jomon, waiting outside, added that half the coaching crowd only joined because they were already keen. Reena looked thoughtful. I suggested she try the school's free Saturday doubt-clearing class for a month and compare her own marks, and offered to meet her parents together with her if she still wants.

qa.a: Eleven students in her section go to the evening coaching centre.

passage: In Berlin, Sami's school published a chart: students who took private tutoring scored higher in the final exams. Sami showed it to his classmate Clara in the corridor. "That's it. I'm getting a tutor. The chart says tutoring works." Clara, who liked statistics, looked closely. "Who takes private tutoring here?" "People who want to do well?" "And people whose parents can pay. Kalyani, you asked why I quit the morning coaching after two months, so here's the story. I'm Ramesh.
In Class 9, I noticed every student picked for the science olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching near the bus depot. All five. I thought, that's it, the coaching is the magic. I begged my parents, and they cut other expenses to pay for it.
Two months of waking at five. My marks didn't move. And sitting there, I saw who the others were. Kids who read science books for fun. Kids whose parents could drive them there at dawn. They'd have been picked anyway. The coaching didn't make them keen; keen kids chose the coaching.
I'm not saying coaching never helps. But I saw two things happening together and decided one caused the other. Now, whenever someone says all the toppers do something, I ask: or do toppers just tend to do it?

qa.q: How many students picked for the olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching?
qa.a: All five students picked for the science olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching.

qa.q: Why did the coaching seem like 'the magic' to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh felt excited and hopeful because all five olympiad students went there, and such a neat match felt like proof of cause.

qa.q: What question does Ramesh now ask, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Ramesh asks whether toppers just tend to do something, which checks whether keen students choose the coaching rather than the coaching making them top.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's parents have felt about the two months?
qa.a: They may have felt hopeful at first and then quietly disappointed, having cut other expenses for a change that didn't come.

grounding: Shows a teenager who concluded coaching caused olympiad selection, missing that keen and better-off students did both.
